newsitem.title: CHINA: China party elite begin closed-door plenum.
newsitem.headline: China party elite begin closed-door plenum.

text.p: China's ruling Communist Party elite gathered behind closed doors in Beijing on Monday for an annual plenum, an opportunity to set policy for the next year and to jockey for power and position, Chinese sources said.
"This is a chance for getting the party faithful back together and united behind the party leader," said one Western diplomat.

"It is going to be a Jiang Zemin-fest," he said, referring to the party chief and state president who has been the subject of a mini-personality cult over the past few weeks in an apparent campaign to build up his image and influence.
State media made no mention of the annual meeting of the party central committee and other party elite that is believed to have started as early as Sunday and usually lasts for about three days.

Security was tight, with additional police on duty, around the site of the meeting in the Jingxi Guesthouse at the western end of Changan Avenue, or the Avenue of Eternal Peace, that cuts through central Beijing.
It was not clear whether any personnel changes in the top echelons of the Politburo, China's most powerful decision-making body, or other party organisations would be announced, Chinese sources said.

Diplomats said a reshuffle was unlikely because such changes could upset the current delicate balance of power and alliances in the party central committee and Politburo, with jockeying for position beginning in the run-up to a crucial party congress due late next year.
"They failed last year to get any significant new appointments made and they all know there is a big reshuffle due next year," the diplomat said.

However, Jiang would seize on the plenum as the last chance before the congress, which is held every five years, to underline his role as anointed heir to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who has not been seen in public for more than two years and is fading gradually from the scene, diplomats and Chinese sources said.
Officials have said the meeting would focus on discussing the importance of "spiritual civilisation," communist jargon for values.

Almost two decades of market-oriented economic reform have eroded what Beijing's leaders regard as orthodox Marxist values, and party chief Jiang has made clear that he wants to place his stamp on ideology in China.

"This is good for rallying the party faithful, but it's not very effective for the rest of the Chinese out there," the diplomat said. "It's yesterday's ideology, yesterday's presentation and yesterday's ideas."
The party mouthpiece, the People's Daily, has filled its front-page for several days with examples of model workers and heroes, whom the populace at large should strive to emulate.

However, mention of Beijing bus conductress Li Shuli -- who rises at 4.00 a.m. to make sure she is familiar with major sites along the route so that she can help disoriented passengers -- raises chuckles from city residents.
"No one takes this kind of thing seriously any more," said one Beijing office worker.
Diplomats said Jiang was using the campaign, coupled with a tough line on the media and ideology, to boost his position.
"He is building himself up as the intellectual heir to (Chairman) Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping," said one diplomat.
